Franz Liszt. The Hungarian composer and teacher who was the most celebrated piano virtuoso of the nineteenth century.

Renowned for his unparalleled technical brilliance and dramatic showmanship, Liszt generated a frenzy among audiences known as Lisztomania. During this intense public hysteria surrounding his concerts in the 1840s, fans fought over his discarded gloves and locks of hair. It was an early precursor to modern celebrity culture.

As a composer, Liszt was a key figure of the New German School. He invented the symphonic poem, a single-movement programmatic orchestral work. He wrote thirteen such works, including Les Préludes, to translate literary and philosophical programs into orchestral sound without classical symphonic divisions.

His keyboard works pushed piano technique to its physical limits. His Piano Sonata in B minor is his single-movement masterpiece, celebrated for its structural innovation where a handful of short motifs are transformed to serve as the themes for all the traditional sections of a sonata.

The Transcendental Études are a set of twelve extremely challenging studies, including Mazeppa and Feux follets. La Campanella, The Little Bell, is his notoriously difficult étude in G-sharp minor. It adapts the bell-like violin harmonics of Niccolò Paganini's Second Violin Concerto.

Liszt wrote a set of nineteen Hungarian Rhapsodies, piano works based on Hungarian folk and Romani melodies. The most notable, Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2, is highly popular and virtuoso.

He was a generous patron and friend to many composers, helping to establish the careers of Hector Berlioz, Edvard Grieg, and Camille Saint-Saëns. His personal relationships were highly publicized, including a long affair with the author Countess Marie d'Agoult, with whom he had three children, and Princess Carolyne zu Sayn-Wittgenstein.

In the middle of his career, Liszt served as the court director of music during the Weimar period, where he championed the works of contemporary composers and mentored pupils from all over Europe for free.

In 1865, Liszt received the title Abbé after moving to Rome, taking minor orders in the Catholic Church and composing sacred choral music. His daughter Cosima eventually married his close friend and protégé, Richard Wagner, creating a complex musical dynasty.
